question: How wide are the court lines, and what's the call when a shuttle lands on a line?

ITTO 8.4 (1) bears on the line judge's action when the shuttle lands in but does not itself answer either part, so it goes in related_sentences.
answer.answer: The court lines are 40 mm wide [1]. A shuttle that lands on a line is in, because all the lines form part of the area which they define [2], and a fault is called only when the shuttle lands outside the boundaries, that is, not on or within the boundary lines [3][4]. When the shuttle lands in, the Line Judge says nothing but points to the line with the right hand while looking towards the Umpire [5].

question: How do we check whether a shuttle has the right speed?

answer.reasoning: The question has one part: how a shuttle is checked/tested to determine whether it has the right (correct) speed. The Laws of Badminton answer this directly in Law 3 'Testing a shuttle for speed': Clause 3.1 sentences (1) and (2) describe the stroke used to test (full underhand stroke, contact over the back boundary line, hit at an upward angle parallel to the side lines), and Clause 3.2 sentence (1) gives the pass criterion (lands not less than 530 mm and not more than 990 mm short of the other back boundary line, per Diagram B). The ITTO clauses (3.5.4.2, 3.5.4.4, 3.6.3) bear on how the referee assesses and monitors shuttle speed but do not add to the testing method itself, so they go in related_sentences. No further search is needed; every part is answered by the sources found.
answer.answer: To check whether a shuttle has the right speed, a player uses a full underhand stroke that makes contact with the shuttle over the back boundary line [1], hitting it at an upward angle in a direction parallel to the side lines [2], and a shuttle of correct speed will land not less than 530 mm and not more than 990 mm short of the other back boundary line [3]. When assessing the result of the shuttle test, take into account the manner in which the shuttles were hit and whether they were hit from the correct location over the back line [4], and all available speeds shall be tested from both ends of the court [5]. The Referee shall at all times when observing play consider whether the shuttle speed selected before play started still appears to be correct [6].

Law 11.4 'Sequence of serving' answers it directly: sentence (1) of laws-11.4 states that in any game the right to serve passes consecutively, and the five list items laws-11.4.1 through laws-11.4.5 give the exact order — from the initial server, to the partner of the initial receiver, to the partner of the initial server, to the initial receiver, and back to the initial server and so on. Each list item is a single numbered sentence (1). Law 11.3.2(2) (the receiving side becomes the new serving side when it wins a rally) bears on when the right to serve passes but does not state the order, so it goes in related_sentences.
answer.answer: In any game, the right to serve shall pass consecutively [1]: from the initial server who started the game from the right service court [2], to the partner of the initial receiver [3], to the partner of the initial server [4], to the initial receiver [5], and then to the initial server and so on [6]. The receiving side shall then become the new serving side [7].

answer.reasoning: The question has one part: the minimum rest a player is entitled to between two matches. The Instructions to Technical Officials clause 3.5.17.4 answers it directly: sentence (1) gives the standard minimum of a 60-minute interval between matches, reducible by the Referee in exceptional circumstances to no less than 30 minutes, and sentence (2) gives the 30-minute minimum for junior, junior team, para badminton tournaments and qualifying rounds. Sentence (3) (Referee should try to provide a longer interval) bears on the topic but does not state the minimum, so it goes in related_sentences. The Laws of Badminton 16.2 intervals concern rest between games within a match, not between matches, so they do not answer this part.
answer.answer: A player is entitled to a minimum 60-minute interval between two matches [1], though in exceptional circumstances the Referee can reduce this to no less than 30 minutes [1]. question: Who should test the shuttles before the tournament, and which speeds get tested?

answer.reasoning: The question asks two things: (1) who should test the shuttles before the tournament, and (2) which speeds get tested. Part 1 is answered by ITTO 3.5.4(1) (the Referee oversees the testing prior to the start of the first day's play) and ITTO 3.5.4.1(1) (the shuttles should be tested by an active player in the tournament, preferably a male player, or a qualified person approved by the Referee). Part 2 is answered by ITTO 3.5.4.2(1) (all available speeds shall be tested from both ends of the court). Related but non-answering sentences: ITTO 3.5.4.3(1) (instructing the tester), ITTO 3.5.4.4(1) (assessing the test result), and Law 3.1/3.2 (how a shuttle is tested and what a correct speed is) describe the test itself but not who tests or which speeds.
answer.answer: Prior to the start of the first day’s play, the Referee shall oversee the testing of shuttles [1], and the shuttles should be tested by an active player in the tournament, preferably a male player, or a qualified person approved by the Referee [2]. All available speeds shall be tested from both ends of the court [3]. The Referee may instruct the shuttle tester during the test, if necessary, such that the shuttles are being tested correctly [4]. When assessing the result of the shuttle test, the manner in which the shuttles were hit and whether they were hit from the correct location over the back line should be taken into account [5]. To test a shuttle, a player shall use a full underhand stroke which makes contact with the shuttle over the back boundary line [6], the shuttle shall be hit at an upward angle and in a direction parallel to the side lines [7], and a shuttle of correct speed will land not less than 530 mm and not more than 990 mm short of the other back boundary line [8].

citations.quote: Prior to the start of the first day’s play, the Referee shall oversee the testing of shuttles.
The shuttles should be tested by an active player in the tournament, preferably a male player, or a qualified person approved by the Referee.

Instruct the shuttle tester during the test, if necessary, such that the shuttles are being tested correctly.

To test a shuttle, a player shall use a full underhand stroke which makes contact with the shuttle over the back boundary line.

question: What does a black card mean, and who decides to give it?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) what a black card means, and (2) who decides to give it. Part 1 is answered by ITTO 5.17.5, which states that when the Referee decides to disqualify the offending player or pair, a black card is given to the Umpire, who calls the player 'disqualified for misconduct' while raising the black card above the head (sentences 1, 3, 4); Laws 16.7.2 sentence 1 confirms the disqualification power, and ITTO 3.6.2.2 sentence 1 states the consequence (disqualified from all events of the tournament). Part 2 is answered by ITTO 5.17.5 sentence 1 ('When the Referee decides to disqualify...') and Laws 16.7.2 sentence 1 ('the Referee, who shall have the power to disqualify the offending side from the match') — the Referee decides; the Umpire only administers/raises the card. Related: ITTO 5.17.4 sentence 5 (umpire must call the Referee on court and report immediately after a red card) bears on how the decision reaches the Referee without answering either part directly.
answer.answer: A black card means disqualification for misconduct: when the Referee decides to disqualify the offending player or pair of players, a black card is given to the Umpire [1]. The Umpire then calls "Come here" to the offending player or pair, announces "[name of player(s)], disqualified for misconduct" followed by a specific explanation of the misconduct, and at the same time raises the right hand holding the black card above the Umpire's head [2][3]. The Referee is the one who decides to give the black card, because on faulting a side (Law 16.7.1.2 or 16.7.1.3) the umpire reports the offending side immediately to the Referee, who has the power to disqualify the offending side from the match [4]. When the Referee disqualifies a player, that player is disqualified from all events of the tournament and, in Team Tournaments, from all future matches of the Team Tournament [5]. The Umpire must call the Referee on court and report immediately [6].

question: What's the rule when a shuttle from the next court rolls onto ours during a rally?

answer.reasoning: The question asks one thing in two aspects: (1) whether a shuttle coming onto the court from an adjacent court during a rally is automatically a 'let', and (2) when a 'let' is or is not called in that situation. The direct answer is in the Instructions to Technical Officials, clause 5.9.1.2: sentence (1) says such a shuttle is not automatically a let, and sentence (2) says no let is called if, in the Umpire's opinion, the shuttle has not obstructed or distracted the players. The Laws of Badminton contain no clause specifically about a foreign shuttle entering the court; the nearest Laws provisions are Law 14.2.7 (a let for any unforeseen or accidental situation) and Law 14.1 ('let' halts play), which I place in related_sentences since they bear on the question without answering the specific part.
answer.answer: A shuttle coming onto the court from an adjacent court during a rally is not automatically a "let" [1]. A "let" is not called in such circumstances if, in the opinion of the umpire, the shuttle has not obstructed or distracted the players [2]. A "let" is called by the umpire, or by a player if there is no umpire, to halt play [3].

question: In wheelchair badminton, what's the rule about lifting off the seat when I hit the shuttle?
